prompt: Ana's folder holds report.txt, report-v2.txt, report-v2-final.txt, report-v2-final-bruno.txt and report-FINAL.txt. Which question can the folder answer on its own?
hint: Look at what `ls -l` printed beside each name.

choices.text: Why the sales figure in FINAL went from 6% to 5%
choices.why: No copy records a reason. The figure changed and the file is silent about it.

choices.text: Which copy was saved most recently
choices.why: Right — the dates are on the files. That is close to all the folder records.

choices.text: Who changed the sales figure in FINAL
choices.why: The owner column says ana for all five, because they all live on Ana's machine.

choices.text: Which copy contains both people's changes
choices.why: None does, and the folder cannot tell you that either. It took two diffs to find out.

prompt: FINAL changed line 2 of the report. Bruno's copy, made from the same starting point, changed line 3. What happens when somebody sends FINAL to the board?
hint: Compare what each copy was made from, not which one is newer.

choices.text: It goes out without Bruno's line, and nothing warns anybody
choices.why: Right. Neither copy has both changes, and a folder has no idea that the two ever diverged.

choices.text: It includes Bruno's line, since FINAL is the newer file
choices.why: Newer is not the same as combined. FINAL was copied before Bruno's change existed.

choices.text: The folder refuses to hold two copies with different content
choices.why: A folder holds whatever it is given. Nothing compares the files in it.

choices.text: Bruno's copy is used instead, because his name is on it
choices.why: His name is in the filename because he typed it there. It gives the copy no authority.

prompt: Which of these does a folder of dated copies lose? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are about the changes. One is about the versions themselves.

choices.text: The reason each change was made
choices.why: Yes. A copy keeps the text and never the sentence explaining it.

choices.text: The old versions of the file
choices.why: This is the one thing copies do keep. It is why people make them.

choices.text: Who made each change
choices.why: Yes. Every copy on Ana's machine is owned by Ana, whoever edited it.

choices.text: Which files were changed together
choices.why: Yes. A copy of one file says nothing about the forty others that changed with it.

prompt: A backup answers "can I get the old one back?". Version control also records who made each change, when, and ___ it was made.
hint: The question the diff could not answer.

prompt: A website has forty files. Before a redesign, Ana copies index.html to index-old.html, then changes index.html, style.css and menu.html. The site breaks, and she copies index-old.html back over index.html. What does she have now?
hint: Count the files that changed, and the files that were copied.

choices.text: Tuesday's site exactly, since the page that broke is restored
choices.why: Only one of the three changed files came back. The page is old and its stylesheet and menu are new.

choices.text: An old page running with the new stylesheet and menu
choices.why: Right. She kept a copy of a file, not the state of the project, so she cannot get back to how all three looked together.

choices.text: Nothing usable, because copying over a file deletes its history
choices.why: The copy worked. The problem is what it did not cover.

choices.text: The redesign, because index-old.html was overwritten too
choices.why: She copied from index-old.html, not onto it. It still holds the old page.

prompt: Each line of a `git log -1` entry answers one question. Match them.
hint: One of the questions on the right is not answered by any line.

pairs.left: Name the quarter in the title

prompt: Ana and Bruno each have a copy of the repository. Why do both copies show the same id, d03056f, for Ana's latest commit?
hint: Where could an id come from, if nobody hands them out?

choices.text: It is computed from what the commit holds
choices.why: Right. The same content, author, date, message and parent give the same forty characters on any machine.

choices.text: A server gives out ids, and every copy asks it for them
choices.why: That is how a central system would do it. Git's ids need no server at all.

choices.text: Git numbers commits in order, so the fourth one matches everywhere
choices.why: A number in order would clash the moment two people committed separately. These are hashes.

choices.text: The ids are random, and cloning copied the random value along
choices.why: Cloning does copy the commits, but the ids are not random. Anybody can recompute them from the content.

prompt: In his copy, somebody changes only the message of Ana's first commit, 32507e0. What happens to the ids of the three commits after it?
hint: Each id is computed over something the commit names.

choices.text: Nothing, since no file changed and only files go into the id
choices.why: The message goes into the id, and so does the parent's id.

choices.text: All three get new ids, because each covers its parent's
choices.why: Right. The first commit's id changes, so the next one names a different parent and changes too, all the way up.

choices.text: Only the edited commit changes; the others keep theirs
choices.why: The others would keep pointing at the old id, which no longer exists. Their own ids include that pointer.

choices.text: Git refuses, because a saved message cannot be edited
choices.why: It can be done, and lesson 4 shows ways that do exactly this. What it cannot do is go unnoticed.

prompt: Ana's newest commit changed only the title line of report.txt. The repository also holds regions.csv. What does that commit's tree list?
hint: A commit is a picture of the project, not of the change.

choices.text: Both regions.csv and report.txt
choices.why: Right. Every commit is a complete snapshot of every file in the project.

choices.text: Only report.txt, since it was the only file that changed
choices.why: That is the diff picture of a commit. The tree names every file, changed or not.

choices.text: Only the new title line of report.txt
choices.why: Lines are what a comparison shows. A commit keeps whole files.

choices.text: Nothing, since trees are only written for a first commit
choices.why: Every commit has a tree. It is the first line of `git cat-file -p`.

prompt: regions.csv has the same blob id, 8ad7960, in the trees of two commits in a row. What does that tell you?
hint: An id is computed from content.

choices.text: Git stored the file twice, once in each commit
choices.why: The same content hashes to the same id, and Git keeps one object per id. Both trees point at it.

choices.text: The same person made both commits
choices.why: The author is in the commit, not in the file's id. These two were made by different people.

choices.text: The file was changed and changed back inside one commit
choices.why: A commit only sees the result. Nothing in the id records steps in between.

choices.text: Its content is the same, so it is kept once
choices.why: Right. That is how a full snapshot every time stays small: an unchanged file is never stored twice.

prompt: `git log --oneline` printed these newest first. Put them in the order they were made, oldest first.
hint: The log reads the chain from the newest end.
items: Use the corrected sales figure from finance
Say by how much the north missed, and add the table it comes from
Name the quarter in the title
trap: Reading the log from the top gives the reverse order: the first line is the most recent commit.

prompt: A team uses Git and keeps a shared copy of its repository on a server. The server's disk fails and there is no backup. Where else is the full history?
hint: What did the clone in this section contain?

choices.text: Nowhere, because the server was the only copy of it
choices.why: That is true of a central system. Every Git clone holds every commit.

choices.text: In every clone on the team's machines
choices.why: Right. Each clone is a complete history, so a team of five has five of them.

choices.text: In the hosting company's archive
choices.why: There may or may not be one. The team does not need it, because they each have the history.

choices.text: Only in the clone of whoever pushed last
choices.why: Every clone has the commits it has fetched, not just the last pusher's.

prompt: A company uses Subversion, a central system, and its server goes down for an afternoon. What can a developer still do?
hint: Where does a central system keep the history?

choices.text: Save versions locally and send them when the server is back
choices.why: That is Git's arrangement. In Subversion a version is saved by sending it to the server.

choices.text: Read the log, since the working copy holds it
choices.why: The working copy holds one version of the files. The log is on the server.

choices.text: Edit files, but neither save a version nor read the history
choices.why: Right. The files are on the machine and everything about their history is not.

choices.text: Nothing at all, including editing files
choices.why: The files are there and can be edited. It is the history that is out of reach.

prompt: Which of these does Git itself do, on a machine with no hosting account? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them needs somebody else to read it.

choices.text: Save a version of the project with a message
choices.why: Yes. A commit is local, and it needs no account.

choices.text: Open a pull request for a colleague to review
choices.why: A pull request is a feature of the hosting service. Git has no idea what one is.

choices.text: Show every commit ever made in the repository
choices.why: Yes. The whole history is on the machine.

choices.text: Compare two versions of a file
choices.why: Yes. Git compares two snapshots it already has.

prompt: Ana clones her team's repository, then spends a week somewhere with no network. What can she not do that week?
hint: Everything about the commits she already has is on her disk.

choices.text: Read the log of commits made before she left
choices.why: Those commits came with the clone. The log reads them from her disk.

choices.text: Save her own changes as commits
choices.why: Committing is local. She can make as many as she likes and share them later.

choices.text: See the commits her colleagues make while she is away
choices.why: Right. Those exist only on their machines and the shared copy until she fetches them.

choices.text: Compare today's files with last month's
choices.why: Last month's snapshot is in her clone. The comparison needs nothing else.

prompt: The command that makes a copy of a repository, with every commit in it, is git ___.
hint: It is the word the section used for the copy it deleted the original of.

prompt: A team agrees to share its work through one repository on GitLab. What makes that copy different from the one on each developer's laptop?
hint: Ask what Git knows about it.

choices.text: It is the only copy that holds the whole history
choices.why: Every clone holds the whole history. That is what distributed means.

choices.text: Git sends every new commit to it automatically
choices.why: Nothing is sent until somebody chooses to share. That is lesson 7.

choices.text: Its ids are the originals, and every clone's are copies
choices.why: An id is computed from content, so there is no original. The same commit has the same id everywhere.

choices.text: The team's agreement; to Git it is one more repository
choices.why: Right. Git treats it like any other copy. The team decided it is the one to meet at.

prompt: Ana's first `git commit` on a new machine stopped with "Author identity unknown". What was missing?
hint: Every commit records something Git would not invent.

choices.text: An account on GitHub that Git could log in to
choices.why: Git never asked about GitHub. A commit is made on the machine, with no account anywhere.

choices.text: A branch called main instead of master
choices.why: The branch name only produced a hint. It did not stop anything.

choices.text: Her name and e-mail address in Git's settings
choices.why: Right. Every commit records who made it, Git would not invent that, and nothing had been set.

choices.text: A file with at least one line of text in it
choices.why: notes.txt had a line in it, and `git add` had accepted it.

prompt: What checks that the address in user.email is really yours?
hint: Think about what the section said a commit does with it.

choices.text: Git, by sending a confirmation message to it
choices.why: Git sends no mail. It has no way of knowing whether the address exists.

choices.text: GitHub, at the moment the commit is made
choices.why: GitHub is not involved when a commit is made. The commit happens on your machine.

choices.text: The operating system, against your account
choices.why: The account name only appeared in Git's failed guess, ana@vm.(none).

choices.text: Nothing: Git just copies it into commits
choices.why: Right. It is not a login. That is why it should be an address you are happy to see published.

prompt: Ana wants her work address on commits in the office repository, and her personal address everywhere else. What does she do?
hint: One of the two settings applies to one place.

choices.text: Set both with --global, running the work one last so that it wins there
choices.why: --global is one value for the whole account. The second command replaces the first everywhere.

choices.text: Everyday one with --global; office one run inside that folder without it
choices.why: Right. A setting made inside a repository applies there, and beats the global one.

choices.text: Keep two .gitconfig files in her home directory and swap them when she changes project
choices.why: It would work until the day she forgot to swap. Git already has a place for per-repository settings.

choices.text: Write the work address at the end of each commit message she makes in that one
choices.why: The message is the reason for the change. The author's address is recorded separately, from the settings.

prompt: Match each setting to what it decides.
hint: One description on the right is something Git never stores in this file.

pairs.right: The name written into every commit
The address written into every commit
What the first branch of a new repository is called
The program Git opens for a longer message

right_distractors: The password Git uses to reach the server

prompt: ~/.gitconfig says defaultBranch = main, and `git config --global --list` prints init.defaultbranch=main. What is going on?
hint: Two spellings, one setting.

choices.text: The file and Git disagree, and the file wins
choices.why: They agree. It is the same setting printed in another case.

choices.text: Names of settings ignore case
choices.why: Right. defaultBranch and defaultbranch are the same name to Git.

choices.text: There are now two settings, one for each spelling
choices.why: The list shows one line for it. There is one setting.

choices.text: The list shows a default Git ships with, not the file
choices.why: Git ships no default for this, which is why the hint appeared. The value came from the file.

prompt: Without the ___ option, `git config` sets a value only for the repository you are standing in.
hint: It is the option that means "for my account, everywhere".

prompt: Starting from a commit's id, put in order what Git reads to get the contents of report.txt as it was in that commit.
hint: The commit names one thing, and that thing names the files.
items: The tree that commit points at
The entry for report.txt in that tree
trap: The commit does not hold files directly. It names a tree, and the tree names the file contents.

prompt: A team keeps its project on a shared drive and copies the whole folder, with the date in its name, every evening. Which question can they still not answer?
hint: Their copies are complete. What is missing from each one?

choices.text: What the whole project looked like on Tuesday evening
choices.why: Tuesday's folder is exactly that. Whole-folder copies do keep the state of the project.

choices.text: Which files differ between Tuesday and Wednesday
choices.why: Two complete folders can be compared, file by file, with nothing else.

choices.text: Why a particular line changed during Tuesday
choices.why: Right. No copy records a reason, and a day's worth of changes collapses into one snapshot with no author and no sentence.

choices.text: Whether Tuesday's project can be put back
choices.why: It can. That is what the copy is for.

prompt: Which of these are true of a Git commit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the five describe the belief this lesson corrected.

choices.text: It records every file of the project, changed or not
choices.why: Yes. Its tree names every file, and unchanged ones point at content already stored.

choices.text: It stores only the lines that changed
choices.why: That is the diff picture. The diff is worked out from two snapshots when you ask.

choices.text: It names the commit made before it
choices.why: Yes. The parent line is what makes a set of saves into a chain.

choices.text: Its id is handed out by the shared server
choices.why: The id is computed from the commit's contents, on whatever machine made it.

choices.text: Its id would change if its message changed
choices.why: Yes. The message is part of what is hashed.

prompt: Which of these is Git, rather than a service built on it?
hint: One of them works with no account and no network.

choices.text: The website where a team opens pull requests
choices.why: That is the hosting service. Git has no web page and no pull requests.

choices.text: The company that keeps the team's shared copy
choices.why: GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are companies. Git is not.

choices.text: The program that records commits on your machine
choices.why: Right. Git is that program, and everything else is built around a copy it made.

choices.text: The account that decides who may send work to the shared copy
choices.why: Accounts and permissions belong to the host. Git has neither.

prompt: Each commit's id is computed over its ___'s id as well, so rewriting an old commit changes the id of every commit made after it.
hint: The line in `git cat-file -p` that names another commit.
